The post Review: Firestone Walker Oktoberfest 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Break out the lederhosen and get the pretzels in the oven! October is here and it’s time to celebrate all things German.

This year’s brew is a collaboration between Firestone Walker and Mahrs Bräu, a brewery in Bamberg (originator of smoky rauchbier) that is 356 years old. It’s fully brewed with German ingredients aside from California water — including Bamberger Pilsen malt, Mahrs Bräu’s own malt, and Hallertau Tradition and Hersbrucker hops — a Festbier designed to emulate what drinking beer in October (really September) in Germany tastes like.

The results are, as expected, uncanny. It really tastes like an authentic German lager, quite malty and ever so lightly fruity with notes of baked apples and banana. Chewy with decidedly moderated bitterness, the gentle sweetness helps the beer feel light as a feather despite its healthy 6% abv. At the same time, the beer has plenty of fest-friendly gravity, offering a rounded, mouth-filling exuberance that ensures a delightful pairing with everything from schnitzel to spätzle and beyond — or just drinking on its own.

6% abv.

A- / $12 per 4-pack of 16 oz cans

title: Review: Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof Bourbon 5 Years Old
summary:
Last summer, we got our first taste of Smokeye Hill, the buzzy Colorado Springs-based whiskey brand notable for the use of heirloom blue corn in their whiskey recipes. David had a chance to review their impressive barrel proof rye whiskey in the fall, and now we’re finally getting to the third, and perhaps most talked…

The post Review: Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof Bourbon 5 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Last summer, we got our first taste of Smokeye Hill, the buzzy Colorado Springs-based whiskey brand notable for the use of heirloom blue corn in their whiskey recipes. David had a chance to review their impressive barrel proof rye whiskey in the fall, and now we’re finally getting to the third, and perhaps most talked about, whiskey in their lineup.

Like the standard bourbon, Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof is distilled on contract from a four-grain mashbill of yellow corn, rye, malted barley, and heirloom blue corn, a nod to the brand’s southwest origins that reportedly makes up more than 50% of the recipe. That spirit ages for at least five years in a mix of 30- and 53-gallon barrels with varying char levels from No. 2 to all the way up to No. 5, a full minute or more of charring that borders on incineration. While the base spirit remains unchanged in each cask, that unique barrel program presumably gives blenders a broader maturation profile to work with. Let’s see how it all works at full strength.

Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof Bourbon 5 Years Old Review

There’s quite a bit of ethanol at the outset here, and like the standard bourbon, some youthful notes come through initially. Grain-forward hints of warm cornbread and a little blue corn grist add a slightly savory edge to things but give way rather quickly to sweeter toffee, vanilla cream, and chewy caramel. At barrel strength, there’s more sweetness coming through than with the standard bourbon, but it’s dark and caramelized. With even more time in the glass, brown butter, pecan pralines, and caramel corn arrive.

The palate delivers barrel proof heft and heat right out of the gate, kicking off with chili pepper, freshly ground cinnamon, whole clove, and plenty of fresh oak and walnut shells. It’s a peppery warmth that goes straight to the nostrils before hugging the back of the throat. Once things settle down, caramel sauce, dark brown sugar, and dried orange peel fill the midpalate with a generous, silky sweetness. The finish kicks off with an unexpected zip of bright wintergreen and candied pineapple before eroding into an off-dry conclusion of pink peppercorn, oak, barrel char, and a little cigar wrapper. At cask proof, this bourbon demands some patience and comes across just a bit too hot in places. Still, it’s showing a lot of promise. Like the standard bourbon, it would likely do very well in a classic whiskey cocktail.

132.4 proof.

B+ / $90

title: Review: 2021 Quinta da Fonte Souto Syrah
summary:
Syrah is not a grape I associate at all with Portugal, but we live in unsettled times, and as with the rest of the world, wine is shifting, too. From the Alentejo comes this curious bottling of Syrah, the Symington family’s first foray outside its historic home of the Duoro. Quinta da Fonte Souto strategically…

The post Review: 2021 Quinta da Fonte Souto Syrah appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Syrah is not a grape I associate at all with Portugal, but we live in unsettled times, and as with the rest of the world, wine is shifting, too. From the Alentejo comes this curious bottling of Syrah, the Symington family’s first foray outside its historic home of the Duoro.

Quinta da Fonte Souto strategically leverages the significant cooling effect of its mountain location. The entire 511 acre estate is nestled in the Serra de São Mamede mountain range at an elevation of 1640 feet. This elevation is vital, recognized for delivering the naturally cooling influence that imparts the trademark freshness and elegance found in the finished wines. The low-yielding, mature vines of the estate further contribute to the structure and complexity of its wines. This 100% Syrah is matured for 12 months in second-year 400 liter French oak barrels.

Dense and slightly beefy, this could well be a New World syrah, heavy with elements of black, almost charred fruit, alongside anise and dark chocolate. The tannins are intense on this wine, the slightest level of balsamic acidity serving to pull it out of the depths that dominate the experience. Greenery rings the edges of the wine, first fresh parsley and rosemary, later a touch of pine needles. Raspberry and anise linger on the finish.

Such an odd, unexpected experience — I’m still processing it in the context of Portuguese still wines.

B+ / $48

title: Review: New Riff Sour Mash Single Malt Whiskey 2026
summary:
New Riff produces an impressive complement of bourbon and rye, but its lone single malt is one of its most unusual and interesting whiskeys, inspired by the barleys used in beer brewing. A vatting of malts that has changed for each of the four years it’s been produced, this evolutionary offering remains as wild and…

The post Review: New Riff Sour Mash Single Malt Whiskey 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
New Riff produces an impressive complement of bourbon and rye, but its lone single malt is one of its most unusual and interesting whiskeys, inspired by the barleys used in beer brewing. A vatting of malts that has changed for each of the four years it’s been produced, this evolutionary offering remains as wild and crazy an experience as ever.

For 2026:

New Riff’s Single Malt Whiskey is comprised of six mashbills aged in five different cask types, marking this expression as one of the distillery’s most intricate blends to date. This year’s blend introduces Chevallier, an 1800s heirloom British malt variety, making its debut in New Riff’s Single Malt distillate for the first time. Distilled using the unmistakable Kentucky regimen — sour mash, open fermentation, and a column still — this whiskey bridges the time-honored heritage of malted barley with Kentucky tradition, resulting in one of New Riff’s most complex and rewarding whiskeys made yet and showcasing the creativity and technical expertise of its distilling team, while continuing its more than a decade’s long commitment to delivering “A New Riff on an Old Tradition.”

The 2026 Single Malt Whiskey is bottled without chill filtration at 111.7 proof with a mashbill of 100% malted barley which includes 11.7% Marris Otter, 14.1% Golden Promise, 27.7% of a beer-inspired Barleywine, 16.5% Belgian Quadrupel, 18% Scottish peated barley, and 12% Chevallier. The five casks the malt whiskeys matured in include new charred oak, de-charred toasted oak, used bourbon barrels, Spanish oloroso sherry casks, and Pedro Ximenez Sherry casks.

As always, that’s a lot to take in, so let all that percolate a bit while we tuck into a review.

New Riff Sour Mash Single Malt Whiskey 2026 Review

Freshly poured, the complexity of aromas threaten to overwhelm. As with prior releases, this one’s all about dried fruit, lacquered nuts, and furniture polish, the various sherry finishes taking control from the start. Rich aromas of figs and dates are countered by a substantial smokiness — peat, then creosote. Overwhelmingly, the nose is sweet and filled with fruit. Only as you remove the glass from your nose do notes of cereal and grains come into focus.

The palate twists the script a bit, and here a more granary-driven character is evident from the start. It’s chewy and toasty, those dried fruits and peels, almost like marmalade, taking their time to work their way into the fore. Once they do, they don’t let go. The fig and date notes become quite immersive, with smoky peat lingering over the top like a husky layer of fog. PX sherry notes cling to the tongue, while dark chocolate and caramel elements work their way to prominence, most notably on the finish. A pipe smoke character lingers here, finishing in more generally ashy territory.

All told it’s another solid performance, though I feel like the fairly heavy smokiness robs this experience of too much of its subtlety.

117.7 proof.

B+ / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Puffin Drinkwear
summary:
Ladies and gentlemen, beverage coozies have officially entered its vibe-check era, leaving standard neoprene in the space dust of their trajectory, thanks to Puffin Drinkware and their fashion line of alternatives. I doubt tailgaters or BBQ goers ever lamented any shortcomings of the OG perfectly utilitarian rubberized version, but Puffin Drinkware thought we deserved better.…

The post Review: Puffin Drinkwear appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Ladies and gentlemen, beverage coozies have officially entered its vibe-check era, leaving standard neoprene in the space dust of their trajectory, thanks to Puffin Drinkware and their fashion line of alternatives. I doubt tailgaters or BBQ goers ever lamented any shortcomings of the OG perfectly utilitarian rubberized version, but Puffin Drinkware thought we deserved better. One should not waste any opportunity for whimsy and self-expression, especially when you are clinging to a cold beverage for as long as you do in plain sight. They saw the opportunity to fully clothe your beer can or wine bottle in a properly tailored flannel, hoodie or bathrobe and grabbed it by the (mini) shirt sleeves. I might add, with triumph and much glee.

The review started and pretty much ended with the unveiling of two styles in an impromptu focus-group-of-one that elicited the following feedback: “Bwahahah – these are awesome!” There really is not much more to add but allow me to enumerate some of the key reviewer-biased attributes of its awesomeness.

  1. They are super cute.
  2. With over 40 styles, there’s an outfit to suit practically anyone such as flannel shirts, hoodies, lifejackets, collaborations with Peanuts and Liquid Death, sleeping bag, ski jackets, and more.
  3. The attention to detail is worthy. The hoodie has drawstrings and a kangaroo pouch. The bathrobe has a functioning snap, as does the flannel. The Hawaiian shirts have buttons. The pahka hood is trimmed with faux fur.
  4. The insulation performs as it should. I dressed a chilled beer in flannel and a chilled white in the bathrobe and let them linger on the kitchen island throughout the day. After an hour they were both quite near original chilled temperature. And honestly, most beers and wines wouldn’t be sitting that long in a party setting. Within 3 hours they were a little less chill and fully at room temperature at hour 6. (But we would all lose our cool after 6 hours of being left alone, amirite?)
  5. No such thing as having too many. (Did I mention collectibility?)

I can’t tell you what to do, but I am suggesting that a Puffin might brighten up anyone’s day for any occasion, and it’s an attractively priced functional conversation piece. Imagine walking over to refresh your glass of wine and reaching for that classy Sauv Blanc wrapped in a white bathrobe. You can almost hear the slippers shuffling along with it.

I could go on and on, but that would all just be another riff on “Bwahahah – these are awesome.” When you know, you know.

A+ / $15 to $30 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: Jack Daniel’s Distillery Series High Angel’s Share
summary:
Release #17 in Jack Daniel’s wildly varied Distillery Series arrives as a reprise. “High Angel’s Share” first appeared in 2018, when these releases were known as the Jack Daniel’s Tennessee Tasters’ Selection. Like the 2018 expression, the idea here is to bottle Tennessee Whiskey from barrels that experienced very high levels of evaporation. The new expression…

The post Review: Jack Daniel’s Distillery Series High Angel’s Share appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Release #17 in Jack Daniel’s wildly varied Distillery Series arrives as a reprise. “High Angel’s Share” first appeared in 2018, when these releases were known as the Jack Daniel’s Tennessee Tasters’ Selection.

Like the 2018 expression, the idea here is to bottle Tennessee Whiskey from barrels that experienced very high levels of evaporation.

The new expression begins with traditional Jack Daniel’s Tennessee Whiskey laid down in 2016. The whiskey rested atop Coy Hill on the top floor of Barrelhouse 1-13 for a high angel’s share maturation. As the barrels rested in the highest reaches of the barrelhouse, an increased amount of whiskey was lost, presenting a unique and deeply rich concentration of flavors within the remaining spirit.

JD’s Coy Hill releases are some of its most prized, namely for their searingly high abv, and High Angel’s Share 2026 comes across like a baby brother to those releases, at a substantial 69.2 proof. Let’s see how the whiskey compares to those releases and the original High Angel’s Share bottling.

Jack Daniel’s Distillery Series High Angel’s Share Review

Boldly barrel-forward on the nose, the aromatics here are fueled by charred wood and creosote, with sweeter vanilla and baked apple building as you breathe deeply. Though it’s about 9 years old, the whiskey connotes significant age, with mocha notes emerging with greater air time.

The palate is scorchingly hot — if you couldn’t snag a Coy Hill, this will do just as well — and right away it benefits from some water. No need to be shy. I dosed it more than once and never felt it got too watery.

Tempered appropriately, the whiskey takes on a soothing, seductive character that drips with vanilla, milk chocolate, and gentle gingerbread flavors. The whiskey remains wood-forward on the tongue, but never to the extreme the nose suggests, with latent layers of licorice, Maraska cherry, and coffee grounds that all perk up before the gently gravelly finish comes roaring back. The conclusion does leave you with a punch of lingering woodiness, but it’s all quite complementary with what’s come before.

A gem of a bourbon that, I’m sure, will fly a bit under the radar.

138.4 proof. A- / $45 (375ml)

The post Drinkhacker 2026 Wine Cheat Sheet / Vintage Chart appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We goofed and forgot to update the Drinkhacker Wine Cheat Sheet last year, but we’re atoning by getting 2026’s edition out a little early. As always, our cheat sheet and vintage chart is designed to give you some quick shortcuts: When faced with two wines from the same region but different vintages, which one should you grab?

In case you’ve missed the sheet’s prior iterations, the concept is simple: Refer to this handy document to discover, painted in the absolute most general of generalities, whether a vintage of wine from a given region is worth a gamble on. The sheet is designed to be printed out and kept in your wallet, or you can save the PDF for offline use or simply bookmark this page (for the next 12 months). This year almost every region has been updated with new selections, and we’ve trimmed some of the older vintages off the back end.

As always, here’s how to use the cheat sheet: Only the last two digits of a year are included to save space, and the list only rarely reaches back into the pre-WWII era, so anything you see starting with a zero or one is from the 2000s.

All years listed here are considered good to great vintages, but those in green with underlining are the cream of the crop, “classic” years that you should consider the very best on the market. (Why green and underlined? So you can tell the difference whether you use a color or black & white printer.)

Check back next October for the next revision of the cheat sheet!

Cheers!

Specifically, the blend includes: 65% whiskey aged 6 to 12 years,…

The post Review: Stranahan’s Colorado Whiskey Peated Cask appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Stranahan’s Peated Cask is a distillery exclusive available only at its Denver location. It’s a straightforward single malt which completed its initial aging in virgin American Oak before finishing in various casks that previously held whiskey from Islay as well as local peated casks.

Specifically, the blend includes:

  • 65% whiskey aged 6 to 12 years, finished in Islay casks
  • 35% whiskey aged 8 to 11 years, finished in domestic peated whiskey casks

We got a sizeable sample to check out, so we did.

Stranahan’s Colorado Whiskey Peated Cask Review

To kick things off, the nose here is quite mild. Those expecting a smoke bomb may be disappointed. Those uninterested in smoke-heavy experiences will likely find this wholly approachable. A fairly classic construction of malty cereal, toasted almond, and wet leather finds a rather gentle complement in the form of a beach bonfire smoke and a bit of salty seaweed. The smokiness grows stronger on the nose as it develops in the glass, but it never reaches the point where it becomes remotely overwhelming.

The palate hits with more sweetness than initially expected, that malt becoming almost cookie-like, with vanilla overtones and a vague hint of lemon peel. Enduring and chewy, the whiskey develops in glass to showcase elements of coconut and milk chocolate, infused just so with light layers of smoke, here more indistinct than the clearly maritime elements on the nose. Sweetness develops continuously over the course of the experience; by the end the smoke has nearly disappeared altogether, replaced with more touches of lemon and some light floral notes.

Fun stuff, and worth picking up if you visit one of Stranahan’s locations.

94 proof.

A- / $70

title: Review: Heaven Hill Grain to Glass – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Rye (Updated 2026)
summary:
Earlier this year, Heaven Hill dropped three unique expressions that take a step away from the distillery’s existing product line — with new mashbills and an approach that focuses foremost on the underlying grains. The launch of the Heaven Hill Grain to Glass series includes three Kentucky whiskeys (at least to start), including a straight…

The post Review: Heaven Hill Grain to Glass – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Rye (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Earlier this year, Heaven Hill dropped three unique expressions that take a step away from the distillery’s existing product line — with new mashbills and an approach that focuses foremost on the underlying grains. The launch of the Heaven Hill Grain to Glass series includes three Kentucky whiskeys (at least to start), including a straight (rye-heavy) bourbon, wheated bourbon, and rye — all over 6 years old. (All three of these samples were distilled in 2017, so they may be up to 7 years old.)

Let’s allow Heaven Hill to give us the deets:

The craft nature of this unique line of Whiskeys starts at the very beginning – the seed. The idea for the line began over 8 years ago as the brainchild of Heaven Hill Executive Chairman Max Shapira. Max’s passion for quality and transparency in whiskey-making lead to a partnership with seed company Beck’s Hybrids – a fellow family-owned and lead operation based in Indiana since 1937. Each year, our Master Distiller works with Beck’s Hybrids to hand select a unique corn seed varietal that has specific attributes desirable for Heaven Hill Grain to Glass, one of which is choosing seed which is best suited for growth in Central Kentucky. The chosen corn seed varietal is then grown by Peterson Farms on one of two sites in Nelson County, one of which is directly across the street from Heaven Hill’s Bardstown facility. Peterson Farms, a multi-generational family farming company, has been entrusted to take the corn seed varietal and cultivate it into healthy grain that goes into the Heaven Hill Grain to Glass mashbills. Since its founding in 1935, Heaven Hill has prided itself on crafting the highest quality Kentucky Whiskeys. Heaven Hill Grain to Glass honors this legacy and the cherished partnerships which were built on handshakes, not contracts.

“Over the course of the nearly 90 years, since the founding of Heaven Hill by my Dad and his brothers, we have always been cognizant of viewing our business from the long term, developing products that fit into this broad vision,” said Heaven Hill Executive Chairman Max Shapira. “Heaven Hill Grain to Glass incorporates everything our long history and heritage brings to our producing what we believe is the most unique, transparent offering that we have brought to market in our entire history. And that is saying a lot.”

The Bourbon and Wheated Bourbon Whiskeys feature mashbills with higher secondary grain content than Heaven Hill’s traditional Bourbon mashbill and Wheated Bourbon mashbill. Bottled at 107 proof, the Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey expression is comprised of 52% corn, 35% rye and 13% malted barley. Bottled at 121 proof, the Kentucky Straight Wheated Bourbon Whiskey expression is made with 52% corn, 35% wheat and 13% malted barley. The Kentucky Straight Rye Whiskey expression is bottled at 123.2, the only barrel proof expression of the series. It also features a higher rye content than Heaven Hill’s traditional Rye Whiskey mashbill consisting of 63% rye, 24% corn and 13% malted barley. The distillates have been aged over six years at Heaven Hill’s Cox’s Creek rickhouse site. Each product is non-chill filtered and bottled at the ideal proof to allow the characteristics of each unique mashbill to shine.

“Working with Beck’s and Peterson Farms to create Grain to Glass has been an incredible experience,” said Master Distiller Conor O’Driscoll. “We’re proud to have crafted an innovative product – taking it from seed to aged liquid – while still remaining true to the values and legacy of Heaven Hill Distillery.”

Well, I’m excited. Let’s see how all that pans out.

We’re updating this review with additional Grain to Glass whiskeys as they arrive. Note that specialty barrel editions of the GtG series are reviewed on their own page.

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Straight Bourbon 1st Edition (2024) Review

52% corn (Beck’s 6158 varietal), 35% rye, 13% malted barley. Aged 6 years in rickhouse W3 on the 3rd, 4th, and 5th floors. Quite toasty and oaky, with aromatic overtones of roasted grains, mixed fresh herbs (particularly rosemary), and red apple skins. Some nutty walnut shell elements arise with time in glass, along with a substantial tobacco leaf quality. Quite hearty on the palate, with a substantial peanut quality mixing with apple and spice notes — almost like applesauce. The oak remains strong here, as does the rye influence, eventually giving the whiskey an intensely grassy quality and an herbal pop. There’s plenty of lingering peanut butter pushing well into the finish, along with a healthy grind of black pepper and a reprise of clove-heavy baking spice. Very much a frontier-style whiskey that lets the grain do the talking. 107 proof. B / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Straight Bourbon 2nd Edition (2025) Review

Similar approach, with the same mash of 52% corn, 35% rye and 13% malt, but the corn seed is varietal Beck’s 6225. Still 6 years old, aged at the Cox’s Creek rickhouse. Note that proof is down 2 ticks to 105. Quite corn-heavy and toasty on the nose, with ample barrel char evident, followed by notes of rosemary and mint. Time in glass really gets the green herbal notes going, and soon enough they overtake everything else. The palate is sweet and earnest — Corn Pops with honey, a touch of charry burnt marshmallow and a fruitiness that takes its time to build — cinnamon spiced apples, then cherry jam, with a solid caramel punch on the back end, ringed with milk chocolate. Ample char informs the finish, adding a bit of grit to what is otherwise a pretty rockin’ whiskey — and one which, aside from a few similarities, doesn’t really resemble the rocky 1st Edition much at all. Namely lacking is that big peanut punch in the 2024 version, and the bold cereal qualities in the first edition are decidedly tempered here. Is it the corn varietal? The rickhouse? The barrel picks? I got nothing, but I would suggest picking this up if you have the 1st Edition on hand (sadly, I don’t) to do a side by side comparison. 105 proof. A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Wheated Bourbon 1st Edition (2024) Review

52% corn, 35% wheat, 13% malted barley. Quite a different animal, and immediately much more approachable and enticing. The nose features muted spices against an immersive backdrop of honey butter, fresh-cut grass, and cracked black pepper. Increasingly nutty as the whiskey develops in glass, but wholly lacking any overt oakiness. The palate is sweet and, again, loaded with peanut butter and honey notes, with any sense of wood all but hidden away. A light layer of baking spice lingers over a gentle top-note of toasted marshmallow, as a warming heat soothes the throat, evoking notes of hot cocoa. Just a touch of char on the finish. This isn’t a particularly complex bourbon, but it’s a delightful choice for cocktailing — or for deep-diving into what wheated bourbon is all about. I’m not alone here, as this is the only whiskey in the collection that is seeing its price being driven up. 121 proof. A- / $150 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Wheated Bourbon 2nd Edition (2025) Review

Same mashbill as last year’s, but made with Beck’s 6225 corn (same as the 2025 straight bourbon). Still aged for over six years at Cox’s Creek, and bottled at barrel proof — considerably lower in abv than the 2024. Soft and nutty on the nose, this doesn’t present itself as even remotely hot, but rather creamy and dessert-like, exuding aromas of crushed almonds, bergamot, pineapple fronds, and a pinch of dark chocolate. Vanilla and caramel create a soothing palate across a creamy body, with a gentle dusting of ground corn to lift the experience. Time spent exploring the whiskey helps notes of toasted coconut, a touch of milky cafe au lait, and ample cinnamon. The finish is actually a bit racy with some red pepper, and more in line with what I’d expect to find in a rye-flavored bourbon, though it is never in disservice of what’s come before. A hint of smoky coffee bean notes linger on the fade-out. Different, but still solid stuff. 106.6 proof. A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Wheated Bourbon 3nd Edition (2026) Review

This year Heaven Hill dropped three new Grain to Glass releases — all wheated bourbons. We received only the mainline offering; a version aged in French oak barrels and one aged 9 years were also dropped. This year’s whiskey is made with Beck’s 6269 corn but has the same mashbill as 2024 and 2025, spending 6 years in char level #3 barrels at the third, fourth and fifth floors of Warehouses W5 and W6 before bottling. A significant heat kicks things off here, which surprises given this 2026 release is roughly the same abv as last year. Again it’s quite nutty on the nose, but also a little torched, offering aromas of barrel char and clove, followed by coffee grounds. Again this whiskey doesn’t ever connote much of a fruit quality, on nose or palate, remaining with its feet firmly in the realm of torched caramel, chocolate sauce, and pepper. As with the ’25, it hits much closer to a modern rye bourbon than a modern wheater, perhaps owed entirely to the power of those heirloom grains. Water tempers just about everything in the experience, and while that dulls some of its gritty heat, it gives a much more balanced complexion to the whiskey in the end. 107 proof. B+ / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Rye 1st Edition (2024) Review

63% rye, 24% corn, 13% malted barley. Take the pungency of the straight bourbon above and double it, and you’re in the realm of this rye. The nose is a pushy powerhouse, intensely herbal and peppery, like walking through a field of just-cut green grass — backed up by a lumberyard that’s been lightly torched around the edges. No surprises on the palate: The impact of the rye is heavy and immediate, and all-encompassing. Many of the bourbon’s same flavor elements appear here but in variations, most of them scorching on the tongue: Rosemary and thyme, burnt pie crust, heavily browned butter, and just a ton of cloves and black pepper to close things out. While the bourbon hints at fruit elements, the rye does not, tamping them down into near-oblivion. It’s as aggressive a rye as you’ll encounter around these parts — and if the idea was to let the grain do all the talking, that has succeeded admirably. 123.2 proof. B / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Rye 2nd Edition (2025) Review

A different mashbill than 2024: 63% rye, 20% corn, and 13% malt, made with Beck’s Hybrids 6225 corn grown by Peterson Farms on one of two sites in Nelson County, Kentucky. The distillate went into the barrel at 107 proof and was aged for over six years at Heaven Hill’s Cox’s Creek rickhouse site. Considerably lower in abv than the 2024, also. The construction here is wildly different, and the character of the whiskey is divergent as well. A rye-powered nose offers savory notes, heavy with dill this time out, then almond and honey offering some tempering notes. An undercurrent of smoked meat, menthol, and a lingering hospital character add a bit of distraction. Very herbal on the palate, with loads more dill, the whiskey is bready to a fault — though it’s clearly a bit thinner than the 2024 release, thanks to the lower abv. Fruitier notes in the form of apples, then cherries, are followed by a reprise of menthol. The overall presentation is driven by the heavy herbal element, making this all spice, all the time — with all of its other flavor components mild diversions from its single-minded mission. 105.2 proof. B / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

content:
Starlight Distillery has been firing off luxe releases for a few years now, and we’ve been trying to keep up with this Indiana upstart’s releases. It’s not an easy task, as they roll out at a healthy clip. Jacob offered a deep dive into the operation’s 25th anniversary releases earlier this year. We’re back already with a look at two more new drops that you’re likely to find should you go out seeking Starlight.

Starlight Indiana Straight Bourbon 10 Years Old 2026 Review

Round two of Starlight’s 10 year old bourbon is a ten-barrel blend of Starlight’s two sweet mash mashbills, the same 3-grain and 4-grain bills Jacob outlined last year. Copper pot distilled and entered into barrel at low proof, the barrels were aged in Warehouse #2, West Side, the warmest of Starlight’s rickhouses. Oddly this resulted in a considerably lower final proof than in 2025, though it’s still a barnburner at 57.1% abv.

There’s a ton of fruit on the nose this year, cherry (again) set against a backdrop of black tea and weak coffee. The barrel influence isn’t shy, showcasing plenty of fresh oak and anise, sometimes evoking a grittiness that can be a bit mouth-puckering. Notes of orange peel add some needed fruit, with cracked black pepper adding spice. Time in glass helps cinnamon and cardamom notes to gain prominence, while a splash of water improves the overall balance of the expression.

There’s plenty to admire here, though at $250 and up, the value proposition is decidedly questionable. 114.2 proof. B+ / $250

Starlight Mizunara Reserve Bourbon Review 

It’s not quite the same whiskey as Starlight’s Carl T. Huber’s Mizunara Bourbon — or at least, it’s a different batch, with a different name — and with a slightly lower abv (and the same price). This is crafted from Starlight’s traditional sweet mash (mashbill unstated) and 8 years total of maturation split between new oak before a finishing stretch in Japanese Mizunara oak casks.

A much sweeter spin on the Starlight formula, this engages immediately with notes of chestnut and almond paste, soon evoking a floral quality that evokes wholly fitting thoughts of orange and cherry blossoms. Time in glass takes the glass more into sesame territory with a pinch of cigar box character, altogether making for a much softer aromatic experience than you’re likely to have encountered in the world of bourbondom.

The palate is equally nutty and quite sweet, butterscotch and vanilla caramels all melted together into a flavor that’s light in body, warming, and evocative of holiday time with its late-game flavors of dried fruits, pecans, and warm gingerbread all in a swirl. The gentle fruit notes are indistinct, with a fruit salad character that blends nicely with all that spice. Soothing and warming, it’s definitely my favorite of this duo. 110 proof. Reviewed: Batch #3. A / $150
